newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK PSBR seen back in the red in May.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK PSBR seen back in the red in May.

text.p: Britain's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) is expected to have moved back into the red in May after April's surprise surplus but the data will show the trend is improving, analysts say.
The Reuters consensus forecast suggests the government borrowed 3.0 billion stg to make up the shortfall between spending and tax revenues in May.
This compares with a 36 million stg surplus in April and a 3.2 billion stg shortfall in May 1996. The May figures are due for release at 0830 GMT on Tuesday.
"May data are likely to move back into the red but the underlying trend is of further improvement," said James Mackay, UK economist at Painewebber.
"The PSBR has been slow to benefit from economic recovery but signs of a revival in tax revenues are now starting to appear."

April was a major tax gathering month and corporation tax receipts in particular swelled the government's coffers, although they were still running marginally below the corporation tax take in April 1996.
Other tax revenues were much improved on a year earlier. Income tax was up 10 percent on the year, while customs & excise receipts, which include indirect taxes (VAT), were up 23 percent on the year.

"We have allowed for a slowdown in receipts growth after the very strong April figure with total revenues to be about 6.0 percent higher than last year," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Spending is also expected to show signs of improvement.

In April, spending figures were flattered by proceeds from the second instalment from the sale of the housing corporation loan book and the final instalment from the sale of the Ministry of Defence married quarters. Both of these items counted as negative spending.

"But even stripping these out, outlays were just 0.9 percent higher than the same month last year, suggesting that the impressive spending restraint seen in the second half of last year continues," said Loynes.

He forecast a slight rebound in departmental spending in May to around one percent, although total spending could be depressed by modest privatisation proceeds due to the early repayment of the second call on Railtrack shares due in June.
The published budget forecast for central government receipts is 274.2 billion stg, which requires growth of 5.0 percent compared to the 6.7 percent growth seen last year.
"This leaves a significant overshoot looking likely even before any tax increases which might be included in the July 2 budget," said Loynes.

City analysts have speculated that Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will tighten fiscal policy to the tune of 3.0 billion stg in his first budget, with the corporate sector likely to bear the brunt of tax rises.

Analysts may get some hint about the extent of fiscal tightening later this week when the National Audit Office (NAO) reports on its assessment of the budgetary assumptions made by the previous government.

"That report could give the Chancellor the excuse he wants to justify tax rises in July," said a gilts trader. "But the (gilt) market will not like it if the NAO makes big revisions to the assumptions made last year."
